blocks.text: The response body is the JSON structure a provider actually returns, this topic covers its typical shape in depth, the choices array, the generated message itself, the finish reason, token usage metadata, and how to parse it reliably rather than assuming a fixed, unchanging shape.

This topic covers the choices array and generated message, the finish_reason field and what its values signal, usage metadata reporting token counts, the response ID and echoed model field, and defensively parsing a response rather than assuming it always looks exactly as expected.
1. The Response Body as What Comes Back

blocks.alt: Building on the request body, the response body is what actually comes back

blocks.text: The response body is the structured JSON a provider sends back after processing a request, containing the actual generated content along with metadata about how and why generation ended.
2. The Choices Array

blocks.alt: A choices array contains one or more generated options

blocks.text: Most chat completion responses wrap the actual generated content inside a choices array, this structure allows a single request to potentially return more than one candidate response, though most applications use just the first entry.
3. The Generated Message

blocks.alt: The generated message carries a role and content field

blocks.text: This connects directly to the messages array structure covered in the previous topic, the generated content itself comes back structured the same way, a role, typically assistant, and a content field carrying the actual generated text, ready to be appended directly to your conversation history for the next turn.
4. The finish_reason Field

blocks.alt: finish_reason can be stop, length, or another value

blocks.text: This connects directly to max_tokens and stop sequences, covered in the previous topic, finish_reason tells you why generation actually ended, stop means it completed naturally or hit a stop sequence, length means it was cut off by the max_tokens limit, checking this field explicitly reveals whether a response is genuinely complete or was truncated.

blocks.content: {"headers":["finish_reason Value","What It Means"],"rows":[["stop","Generation completed naturally or hit a stop sequence"],["length","Generation was cut off by the max_tokens limit"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Usage Metadata

blocks.alt: A usage field reports token counts for the prompt and the completion

blocks.text: This connects directly to tokens and tokenization, covered in an earlier module, the usage field reports exactly how many tokens the prompt consumed, how many the completion consumed, and the total, this is the actual, authoritative figure for billing purposes and for tracking real token cost, more reliable than estimating token count yourself.

blocks.title: This is the ground truth figure for cost tracking
blocks.content: Rather than estimating token usage with a separate tokenizer tool, the usage field in an actual response gives the authoritative count the provider will actually bill for that specific request.

blocks.text: 6. Response ID and Echoed Model

blocks.alt: A response ID and the model field get echoed back

blocks.text: This connects directly to the request ID header concept covered in the earlier Headers topic, the response body itself often includes its own unique identifier, along with the specific model that actually processed the request, both useful for logging and later debugging.
7. Defensively Parsing the Response

blocks.alt: Assuming a fixed response shape is compared against defensively parsing the response

blocks.text: This connects directly to output validation, covered in an earlier module, an application should check that expected fields are actually present before accessing them directly, rather than assuming the exact shape will always hold, a provider API change, a genuinely unusual edge case, or a network issue truncating a response can all produce something slightly different than expected.
8. Handling an Empty or Unexpected Response

An empty choices array, a missing message field, or a response that fails to parse as valid JSON at all, all need explicit handling in application code, exactly the same defensive discipline covered in the earlier Output Validation topic, applied here specifically to the raw API response shape.
9. A Worked Complete Response Body

A complete, well formed response includes a unique ID, the model that processed the request, a choices array with the generated message and finish reason, and usage metadata reporting exact token counts, everything an application needs both to use the actual content and to track cost and completeness.
Worked Example

A team building a summarization feature notices occasional truncated summaries that end mid-sentence, initially assuming this is a random model quality issue, checking the finish_reason field on those specific responses reveals they are consistently "length," meaning the response was cut off by an insufficient max_tokens setting, not a quality problem at all.

Increasing max_tokens to accommodate genuinely longer summaries resolves the issue entirely, demonstrating how checking finish_reason explicitly reveals the actual root cause rather than misdiagnosing a configuration issue as a model quality problem.
Common Mistakes

items: Not checking finish_reason, missing that a response was truncated by the length limit rather than completing naturally
Assuming a fixed response shape without defensively checking that expected fields are actually present
Estimating token usage yourself instead of using the authoritative usage field the response actually provides
Ignoring the response ID, losing a valuable reference for later debugging or support requests

blocks.text: Practice

Take a real or simulated API response, write parsing code that checks for the presence of choices, message, and usage fields defensively before accessing them, and test it against both a well formed response and a deliberately malformed one missing an expected field.
Key Takeaway

The response body carries the generated content inside a choices array, along with a finish_reason explaining how generation ended, authoritative usage metadata for token counts, and identifying information like a response ID and the model used, and parsing this structure defensively rather than assuming a fixed shape holds up against real world edge cases and provider changes.
